comment: The latency bars the project claims, and the benches that measure them.
Every read the server serves answers in under a millisecond, a page of an
expansion included (the owner's bar, 2026-09-05, tightened from the ten
milliseconds #129 set for a page); scripts/checks/bench-bars.sh runs the
benches and fails when a median crosses its bar.
Figures are microseconds: every bar is now met with room to spare, and
milliseconds no longer say anything useful about them.
A bar is the CLAIM, not a machine's measurement: it never moves to match
a slower run. `measured_us` records what one machine answered, so the
headroom a run has is visible, and it is a record, never a gate.
machine: Apple M2 Pro, macOS 25.5, release profile, 20000 synthetic concepts

served_comment: The bar a served read holds across every code system, checked against the
committed record set rather than the synthetic edition, because it is about
what a real system answers with.
A read costs a fixed amount plus the serialising of its answer, at a rate
that is the same on every system. A flat bar across systems is therefore
not a bar on the server's speed: it asks a 63 KB answer to serialise four
times faster than a 1.5 KB one, which is a bar on how much a system has to
say about a concept. So the bar has the shape the measurement has, and a
regression in either term fails it: a slower operation moves the fixed
part, a slower codec moves the rate (the decision on #512).

served_bars.measured: on 2026-09-08, natively: 862 B answered in 75 us, 7,368 B in 123 us, 26,725 B in 211 us, 63,134 B in 355 us, which is a fixed 70 us plus 4.5 ns per byte; the bar above carries headroom over that fit
served_bars.claim: a served read costs a fixed amount plus the serialising of its answer, at one rate on every code system
